Next experiment — Forecast a full seven days

We'll use the last 168 hourly positions as the test window. One of those hours has a missing rental count, so we'll generate a forecast for all 168 hours but evaluate only the 167 hours with known actual values. Timestral supports missing observations in the historical context, and 168 forecast steps fit within a single forecasting block.

  3. The daily seasonal-naive baseline you already evaluated.
  4. A weekly seasonal-naive baseline, which repeats the previous complete week. The last comparison is worthwhile because hourly bike rentals have both daily and weekly patterns.

data.text/markdown: Visualize the calander-aware forecast

Next experiment: holiday and working-day indicators

The UCI dataset includes two useful features that we haven't supplied yet:
  • holiday: whether the date is a holiday.
  • workingday: whether the date is neither a weekend nor a holiday. UCI Machine Learning Repository These are particularly relevant to our December test period. Unlike future weather observations, the holiday and working-day flags can be known before the forecast starts.
Timestral also supports known-future numeric covariates. Binary indicator rows containing only 0s and 1s receive special treatment in the implementation.

data.text/markdown: Rolling-origin backtesting

We'll evaluate four approaches:
  1. Timestral using target history only.
  2. Timestral using calendar categories plus holiday and working-day indicators.
  3. Daily seasonal naive.
  4. Weekly seasonal naive. We'll test 20 seven-day windows spaced 21 days apart, covering approximately 13 months from November 2011 through December 2012. Each window starts on the same weekday and at midnight, and the forecast horizon is always 168 hours. This gives us a more varied assessment of seasonality and holiday effects.

Define the backtesting function

Create one cell containing this function. Variables such as context, actual, forecast, and origin are now local to the function, so they won't conflict with variables in other notebook cells.
Call the function and unpack its results
